answer:
VIABILITY: The path to revenue is clear but thin. Pricing is simple ($350/ambulance, $750 flat for 3+), software gross margin of ~87% is plausible, and the product addresses a real, well-evidenced pain point (17 of 19 crew members on paper; 11 of 19 unsure about repeat doses). Pilot signals are encouraging (112 logged calls, 6-second median medication log, 4.4/5 report usefulness). However, no paid contract exists. 'Would pay' statements from two directors at free pilot sites are weak evidence of willingness to pay, especially in a segment funded by small operating budgets and annual grants. The core monetization assumption is therefore unproven.

SCALABILITY: The market is small by the team's own estimate (~$3.5M SAM, 10,000 ambulances). At 200 ambulances break-even ($70K revenue) the company is a lifestyle-scale or niche business unless it expands. Adjacent segments (rural career services, critical access hospital transfers) are acknowledged as unvalidated, so growth beyond the wedge is speculative. The proposed channel, state and county volunteer EMS associations, is smart: it offers one-to-many endorsement and low CAC if it works. But association sales cycles are slow, endorsement is not purchase, and the team has no signed partner yet. Onboarding includes a 90-minute training and protocol configuration per agency, which is manual and will strain a four-student team as agency count grows; this undermines the 87% margin once support, configuration, travel and hardware logistics are counted (the $45/ambulance cost estimate looks optimistic).

ASSUMPTIONS: (1) Adoption speed: 40 ambulances/16 agencies in year one against only 2 pilot sites is aggressive given long volunteer-agency decision cycles; the plan itself admits pilots only partly support it. (2) Grant funding of subscriptions is central to sales but unvalidated; grant cycles are annual and competitive, which delays revenue and may recur as a renewal risk. (3) Year-three break-even at ~200 ambulances implies ~5x growth after a first year that has not been tested. (4) Year-one expenses (~$38K) far exceed revenue (~$12K), so the business depends on outside capital, and the $25K ask only partially covers the gap, with no stated plan for subsequent funding. (5) The competitive assessment (incumbents ignoring small agencies) is plausible but untested; a free or low-cost offline mode from an incumbent or a state-sponsored tool could undercut pricing. (6) Regulatory exposure (PHI/HIPAA, state EMS data reporting standards, possible medical-device or protocol liability for dose timers) is treated as a minor item with $2.5K budgeted and no compliance expertise on the team; this could block hospital adoption and delay sales.

STRENGTHS OF THE PLAN: Honest about limits (small market, no paid contracts, expense gap); sensible lean design (does less than a full ePCR); founders with domain credibility (volunteer EMS experience, former EMT, nursing input); the use of funds is focused on the right uncertainty (six paid pilots to test willingness to pay).

VERDICT: A credible, well-researched early-stage idea with a defensible niche and a sound validation plan, but the business model is not yet proven and the standalone scale is limited. The decisive next evidence is converting pilots to signed paid subscriptions and getting at least one association channel partner or grant-funded purchase. Without that, revenue projections and break-even timing should be treated as optimistic.
